plan: Complete enhanced-ACT natural-science passage (CLD-P-ACT-R-000043, 'Seconds Ahead of the Shaking'), about 540 words, on earthquake early warning: P vs S wave speeds, how alerts outrun shaking, distance and the blind zone, uses of seconds, Mexico City and Japan, limits (magnitude saturation, false alarms). Topic checked against all ACT Reading and SAT R&W passages (no early-warning passage). Warning-time figures checked arithmetically: S waves at ~3.5 km/s take ~29 s to travel 100 km and ~9 s to travel 30 km, minus a few seconds for detection.

passages.title: Seconds Ahead of the Shaking
passages.text:
In an earthquake, the ground begins to shake only after waves of energy have traveled outward from the fault where rock suddenly slipped. Those waves do not all travel at the same speed. The first to arrive, called P waves, move through rock at roughly six kilometers per second and usually cause only mild shaking. The slower S waves, at about three and a half kilometers per second, and the surface waves that follow them do most of the damage.

Earthquake early warning systems take advantage of this gap. A network of sensors detects the first P waves near the source, computers estimate the quake's location and size within a few seconds, and an alert is sent—by radio, by cell phone, or directly to machinery—to places farther away. Because electronic signals travel almost instantly compared with waves moving through rock, the alert can outrun the damaging shaking.

How much warning a place receives depends on its distance from the source. A city 100 kilometers away might receive fifteen or twenty seconds of notice; a town 30 kilometers away might get only a few. Closest to the source lies what seismologists call the blind zone, where the damaging waves arrive before any alert can be issued.

A few seconds may not sound like much, but the uses are concrete. Trains can begin braking, surgeons can lift their instruments away from patients, elevators can stop at the nearest floor and open their doors, and students can take cover under their desks. Mexico City has operated a public warning system since the early 1990s. The city lies roughly 300 kilometers from the coastal faults that produce many of its strongest earthquakes, which gives it unusually long warnings. Japan's nationwide system sends alerts through television, radio, and phones.

Early warning has limits. A system must estimate an earthquake's size from only the first few seconds of data, and the largest earthquakes can keep growing for a minute or more after they begin, so early estimates may be too low. False alarms are another risk: alerts that turn out to be unnecessary can teach people to ignore later ones. Engineers are working on faster detection and better estimates, but no system can eliminate the blind zone. The gain from early warning is measured not in minutes but in seconds—and in what people manage to do with them.

candidates.stem: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

choices.A: Early warning systems use the speed gap between seismic waves to give seconds of useful notice, though they have real limits.
choices.B: Early warning systems can now predict earthquakes days before they occur, allowing cities to evacuate.
choices.C: Mexico City and Japan have the only earthquake warning systems that work reliably anywhere in the world.
choices.D: P waves cause more damage than S waves, which is why sensors are designed to detect P waves first.

candidates.evidence: Earthquake early warning systems take advantage of this gap.
candidates.explanation: The passage explains the wave-speed gap, how systems use it, what the warnings allow, and their limits.

B.rationale: The systems detect quakes already under way and give seconds, not days, of notice.

C.rationale: The passage describes both systems but never claims they are the only reliable ones.

D.rationale: The passage says S and surface waves do most of the damage; P waves are detected first because they arrive first.

hints: What does most of the passage explain, and how does it end?
candidates.remember: A main idea must cover both the passage's explanation and its qualifications.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, compared with S waves, P waves:

choices.A: travel more slowly and cause most of the damage.
choices.B: travel at the same speed but arrive later.
choices.C: travel faster and usually cause milder shaking.
choices.D: travel faster and cause most of the damage.

candidates.evidence: move through rock at roughly six kilometers per second and usually cause only mild shaking
candidates.explanation: P waves move at about six kilometers per second versus about three and a half for S waves, and they usually cause only mild shaking.

A.rationale: This reverses the passage: P waves are faster and milder.

B.rationale: The passage says the waves travel at different speeds and P waves arrive first.

D.rationale: P waves are faster, but S and surface waves cause most of the damage.

strategy.explanation: Check both parts of each choice.

candidates.remember: Two-part choices are right only if both parts are right.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, an alert can reach a distant city before the damaging shaking does because:

choices.A: S waves stop traveling once they reach the edge of the blind zone.
choices.B: electronic signals travel almost instantly compared with waves moving through rock.
choices.C: sensors are placed in every city so that each can detect its own shaking.
choices.D: P waves travel faster than electronic signals sent by radio or cell phone.

candidates.evidence: Because electronic signals travel almost instantly compared with waves moving through rock
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the alert can outrun the shaking because electronic signals travel almost instantly compared with seismic waves.

A.rationale: The passage does not say S waves stop; the blind zone is where alerts arrive too late.

C.rationale: The sensors detect P waves near the source, not in every city.

D.rationale: Electronic signals are far faster than any seismic wave.

candidates.remember: Cause questions are answered by the reason the passage gives.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, which of the following places would most likely receive the longest warning before damaging shaking from an earthquake?

choices.A: A school directly above the point where the fault slipped
choices.B: A train station about 10 kilometers from where the fault slipped
choices.C: A factory about 40 kilometers from where the fault slipped
choices.D: A hospital about 150 kilometers from where the fault slipped

candidates.evidence: How much warning a place receives depends on its distance from the source.
candidates.explanation: Warning time grows with distance from the source, so the place farthest away, 150 kilometers, would get the longest warning.

A.rationale: This is in the blind zone, where shaking arrives before any alert.

B.rationale: Places this close get little or no warning.

C.rationale: This is farther than 10 kilometers but much closer than 150, so it gets less warning.

hints: What does warning time depend on?
candidates.remember: Apply a stated relationship to new cases rather than looking for the same numbers.

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "concrete" most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: The sentence is followed by specific, practical actions (trains braking, surgeons lifting instruments), so "concrete" means specific and practical.

A.rationale: That is a familiar meaning, but the sentence describes uses of a few seconds, not a building material.

B.rationale: Nothing in the sentence concerns whether the uses can change.

D.rationale: The uses are listed openly; nothing is hidden.

hints: What follows the word in the paragraph?

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning the surrounding sentences support.

candidates.stem: In paragraph 4, the examples of trains, surgeons, elevators, and students mainly serve to:

choices.A: show that even a few seconds of warning allow useful protective actions.
choices.B: explain why Mexico City built its warning system in the early 1990s.
choices.C: suggest that warnings are useful only in buildings with modern equipment.
choices.D: demonstrate that the blind zone has been eliminated in large cities.

candidates.evidence: A few seconds may not sound like much
candidates.explanation: The examples follow the claim that a few seconds have concrete uses and illustrate actions that can be taken in that time.

B.rationale: The examples are general; the paragraph gives a separate reason for Mexico City's long warnings.

C.rationale: Students taking cover need no equipment, so the examples do not suggest this.

D.rationale: The passage later says no system can eliminate the blind zone.

hints: What claim comes right before the examples?

strategy.explanation: Connect the list to the sentence before it.

candidates.remember: Examples usually support the claim that introduces them.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Mexico City receives unusually long warnings mainly because the city:

choices.A: has more sensors than any other city in the world.
choices.B: lies roughly 300 kilometers from the faults that cause many of its strongest earthquakes.
choices.C: sends its alerts by television instead of by cell phone.
choices.D: has operated a warning system longer than any other city.

candidates.evidence: which gives it unusually long warnings
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the city's distance from the coastal faults gives it unusually long warnings.

A.rationale: The passage does not compare numbers of sensors.

C.rationale: How alerts are sent does not affect how much warning there is; the passage says Japan uses television.

D.rationale: The passage gives the system's start date but links long warnings to distance.

hints: What does "which gives it unusually long warnings" refer to?

strategy.explanation: Find the clause that gives the reason.

candidates.remember: Watch for true details that are not the stated reason.

candidates.stem: Based on paragraph 5, early estimates of the size of the largest earthquakes may be too low because:

choices.A: the sensors near the source are usually destroyed by the first P waves.
choices.B: large earthquakes produce no P waves for the sensors to detect.
choices.C: false alarms cause engineers to lower every estimate on purpose.
choices.D: those earthquakes can keep growing well after the first few seconds the system uses.

candidates.evidence: the largest earthquakes can keep growing for a minute or more after they begin
candidates.explanation: Estimates rely on the first few seconds of data, but the largest quakes may keep growing for a minute or more, so the early estimate can fall short.

A.rationale: The passage does not say sensors are destroyed.

B.rationale: All earthquakes in the passage produce P waves, which arrive first.

C.rationale: False alarms are a separate risk; nothing says estimates are lowered on purpose.

hints: What happens to the largest quakes after the first few seconds?

strategy.explanation: Combine the two facts in the same sentence.

candidates.remember: A limitation often comes from a mismatch between the data used and what happens later.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, a person in the blind zone during an earthquake would most likely:

choices.A: feel the damaging shaking before receiving any alert.
choices.B: receive fifteen or twenty seconds of warning before the shaking.
choices.C: feel no shaking at all, since the waves pass beneath the zone.
choices.D: receive an alert but feel only mild P-wave shaking afterward.

candidates.evidence: where the damaging waves arrive before any alert can be issued
candidates.explanation: The blind zone is defined as the area where damaging waves arrive before an alert can be issued, so a person there would feel strong shaking first.

B.rationale: That much warning is described for a city about 100 kilometers away, not the blind zone.

C.rationale: The blind zone is closest to the source, where shaking is strong.

D.rationale: In the blind zone, damaging waves arrive before any alert can be issued.

hints: How does the passage define the blind zone?
candidates.remember: When a passage defines a term, use the definition to predict outcomes.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires applying the blind-zone definition while rejecting a detail about distant cities.

candidates.stem: The final sentence of the passage ("The gain from early warning ... do with them") most strongly suggests that the value of an early warning system:

choices.A: is too small to justify the cost of building such systems.
choices.B: depends on whether people and machines are ready to act in the few seconds it provides.
choices.C: will grow to several minutes once engineers improve detection.
choices.D: is greatest for people living closest to the earthquake's source.

candidates.evidence: and in what people manage to do with them
candidates.explanation: The sentence says the gain is measured in seconds "and in what people manage to do with them," so the benefit depends on readiness to act, as the examples in paragraph 4 show.

A.rationale: The author stresses concrete uses of a few seconds and does not argue the systems are not worth their cost.

C.rationale: The author says the gain is measured in seconds and that the blind zone cannot be eliminated.

D.rationale: People closest to the source are in the blind zone and get the least warning.

hints: What does "what people manage to do with them" add?

strategy.explanation: Connect the last sentence to paragraph 4's examples.

candidates.remember: Concluding sentences often restate the passage's main point in compressed form.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires connecting the final clause to the earlier examples and rejecting claims the passage contradicts.
